body.objective: Students will be able to name body parts.
successCriteria: I can name parts of the body in Spanish
I can use the article with body parts
I can follow and give body instructions
body.hook: La cabeza, los hombros, las rodillas y los pies: you may have sung this as a child. Body vocabulary is essential for sports, fitness and especially for explaining what's wrong at the doctor's.

study.title: El cuerpo humano
study.question: What are the parts of the body in Spanish?
study.passage:
Body vocabulary (written for this lesson): la cabeza, la cara (face), los ojos, la nariz, la boca, las orejas (outer ears) / los oídos (inner ears), los dientes (teeth), la garganta (throat), el cuello (neck), los hombros (shoulders), el brazo, el codo (elbow), la mano, los dedos (fingers), la espalda, el pecho (chest), el estómago, la pierna, la rodilla (knee), el tobillo (ankle), el pie.
Notes: la mano is feminine even though it ends in -o. Spanish usually uses the article (not mi) with body parts: Levanta la mano. Me lavo las manos.
Activities: 1. Label a body diagram. 2. "Simón dice" (Simon says): Simón dice: tócate la nariz. Simón dice: levanta los brazos. 3. Sing "Cabeza, hombros, rodillas y pies." 4. A student leads a stretching routine in Spanish: Levanten los brazos. Doblen las rodillas. Giren la cabeza.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; "Cabeza, hombros, rodillas y pies" is a traditional children's song.
discussion: Which body word has a surprising gender?
What's the difference between orejas and oídos?
How could you use these words in sports?

body.objective: Students will be able to describe symptoms with doler.
body.iCan: I can describe symptoms with doler.
successCriteria: I can describe pain with me duele and me duelen
I can describe other symptoms with tener and estar
I can role-play a doctor's visit
body.hook: "Me duele la cabeza." Like gustar, the verb doler works backwards: the body part "hurts to you." Learn this pattern and you can explain any ache to a doctor.

study.title: En el consultorio
study.question: How do I describe symptoms in Spanish?
study.passage:
Grammar (written for this lesson): doler works like gustar: the body part is the subject. Me duele la cabeza (one part). Me duelen los pies (plural). Te duele, le duele, nos duele(n), les duele(n).
Other symptoms: tener + fiebre / tos / dolor de cabeza / gripe (flu) / náuseas. estar + enfermo/a (sick), resfriado/a (have a cold), cansado/a (tired), mareado/a (dizzy).
Dialogue (read in pairs):
Médica: Buenos días. ¿Qué te pasa?
Diego: No me siento bien. Me duele la garganta y me duelen los oídos.
Médica: ¿Tienes fiebre?
Diego: Sí, un poco. Y tengo tos.
Médica: ¿Desde cuándo?
Diego: Desde hace tres días.
Médica: Tienes una infección de garganta. Toma esta medicina, bebe mucha agua y descansa.
"Desde hace + time" = for (a length of time up to now).
Activity: symptom cards: partners act out symptoms; the other asks ¿Qué te duele? and diagnoses with me duele/me duelen.
study.source: Original dialogue written for this lesson.
discussion: What advice does the doctor give?
study.product: Write a doctor dialogue with at least five symptoms, using me duele and me duelen correctly and one desde hace sentence.

body.objective: Students will be able to talk about feelings with estar.
body.iCan: I can talk about feelings with estar.
successCriteria: I can describe feelings and emotions with estar
I can explain why I feel a certain way with porque
I can give advice for wellbeing
body.hook: "¿Cómo estás?" is more than a greeting. Spanish uses estar to describe how you feel right now: happy, nervous, bored, stressed. Talking about feelings is part of looking after your health.

study.title: ¿Cómo te sientes?
study.question: How do I talk about feelings and wellbeing in Spanish?
study.passage:
Guide (written for this lesson):
estar + feeling (temporary states): Estoy contenta. Estamos nerviosos. ¿Estás cansado?
Feelings agree: nervioso (boy), nerviosa (girl), nerviosos (group). Feliz and triste don't change for gender (feliz → felices in plural).
Note: ser aburrido = to be boring; estar aburrido = to be bored.
Reasons: Estoy nervioso porque tengo un examen. Estoy contenta porque es viernes.
Sentirse: Me siento bien / mal / mejor (I feel well / bad / better).
Wellbeing advice (tú commands): Duerme ocho horas. Haz ejercicio. Habla con un amigo. Respira profundamente. Toma un descanso. Escucha música.
Activity: emotion cards with scenarios (Tienes un examen mañana. Tu mejor amigo se muda. Ganaste un partido.). Partners say how they'd feel, why, and give one piece of advice. Share only what you're comfortable sharing.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: Why is estar used for feelings?
